items.title: Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners
items.standfirst: Senegal ​were reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners ​on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld their appeal against being stripped of the title. Senegal contested the ​Confederation ‌of African Football's decision to declare ⁠Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 after extra time in ‌January's final in Rabat. Morocco announced that it would “pursue all necessary legal procedures” in response to the decision.

items.title: Senegal regain AFCON title after successful appeal at sport arbitration court
items.standfirst: The Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday unanimously ruled in favour of Senegal in the appeal to reclaim the Africa Cup of Nations title, 10 months after a chaotic final against Morocco. Senegal won the match in January but was stripped of the title in March because many of the team's players had walked off the pitch in protest over a penalty given to the opposing side. Morocco said it would contest the ruling.

clusters.title: Zelensky Hails Ukraine's 'Exemplary' Attack on Russian Warship in Libya
clusters.neutral_headline: Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya

items.title: Zelensky Hails Ukraine's 'Exemplary' Attack on Russian Warship in Libya
items.standfirst: Ukraine's President hailed the sinking of the warship as an example of an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war.”
items.content: Vantor satellite image shows a vessel partly visible in the water beside a pier in Benghazi. Scattered debris and darkened areas are visible along the pier on Nov. 22, 2026. —Vantor—Getty ImagesUkraine sank a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya using naval drones, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Forces deployed seven Ukrainian-made drones that struck and sank the Russian corvette Mercury, which was carrying a combat helicopter, Zelensky said Monday. A second ship, the Russian container carrier MV ANGARA, which Zelensky said was being used to “transport weapons,” was also hit.Footage released by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense appeared to show sea drones speeding toward the warship—one of the newest in Russia's fleet—before it erupted into a giant ball of flames.The Mercury was commissioned a year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and incorporates some of Moscow’s latest shipbuilding technology, Russian state news agency TASS reported when the ship joined the fleet in May 2023.Russia’s Defense Ministry has yet to comment on the attack.Zelensky hailed the sinking of the warship as an example of an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war.”Late Monday morning, Zelensky made a virtual appearance at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, where peace opportunities for Ukraine and suspected Russian violations of NATO airspace were top of the agenda.“Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refineries are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking,” Zelensky said as he addressed attendees. “We have offered Russia steps to reduce the fighting dozens, dozens of times, and we have never been the ones to raise the stakes. But, unfortunately, Russia gives us no peaceful response.” The strikes against the corvette, conducted around 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, underscore Kyiv's long-range strike capabilities.The Mercury had been in the port of Benghazi to refuel under a maritime cooperation agreement before its planned return to Russia, according to Libya’s Government of National Stability (GNS). In the wake of the strikes, the GNS, which controls eastern Libya and has a longstanding military relationship with Russia, said it had filed an official complaint with the U.N. Secretary-General and Security Council over threats to maritime security, arguing that the country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war.The U.N. Support Mission in Libya called for an “immediate, independent, and transparent investigation,” offered U.N. assistance, and warned against drawing Libya into a wider confrontation.The Foreign Ministry of the internationally-recognized northwestern Libyan government expressed "grave concern" over the attack, insisting that “the continuation of the war between ‌Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct military operations on ⁠Libyan territory or ​in its territorial ​waters.” U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resumed earlier this month after a nine-month hiatus, but there is still no clear pathway to peace.President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for a historic sit-down at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week. Trump and Putin had a one-on-one conversation on the sidelines beforehand, but all communications failed to produce any meaningful progress toward ending the Russia-Ukraine war.Russian cargo vessel hit by drone in Baltic SeaThe strike in Libya followed a separate drone attack on a Russian cargo vessel in the eastern Gulf of Finland on Saturday, according to Finland's Ministry of Defense.The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck Saturday morning.The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters before being towed out Sunday by a Russian rescue vessel, following a Finnish-led response involving Estonia and Russia.While Kyiv has not claimed responsibility for the attack, Aki-Mauri Huhtinen, director of communications for the Finnish Defense Forces, told local media “it is likely that Ukraine” was behind the strike.TIME has reached out to Ukraine's Defense Ministry for comment.The Kremlin described the attack on the Russia bulk carrier as escalating tensions in international waters. "All coastal countries are certainly concerned about this. This is very dangerous. It is escalating tensions in the region,” said Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, according to TASS.The U.S. Treasury previously sanctioned the Sparta II in 2022, alleging that the vessel was linked to Russian military logistics company Oboronlogistika.NATO “will defend every inch of Polish territory,” says RutteNATO chief Mark Rutte pledged Saturday that the alliance would “defend every inch of Polish territory,” speaking to reporters in Warsaw a day after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Polish territory.Two missiles fell in Polish territory, with one landing near the town of Nowy Lipowiec, in the eastern part of the country, while another missile was discovered in a forest in southeastern Polish territory. Remnants of a drone were also found scattered across the southeastern part of the country.Polish prosecutors said that all three fell in undeveloped areas with no injuries or significant property damage reported. All three areas remain under surveillance."I don't want to leave any room for interpretation—we know for sure that what fell on Polish soil came from Russia," Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed during a press conference. “While there were no casualties or damage, it clearly demonstrates the scale of Russia's attack on Ukraine and the fact that the coming months will be filled with significant challenges.”Russia has not claimed responsibility for the projectiles.A meeting of NATO's North Atlantic Council took place Monday to discuss the violation of Poland’s airspace."It is ⁠clear that this ​is ⁠a dangerous incident. ‌It comes from Russia," Rutte said in Berlin. "Whether it is ⁠intentional or not has to be decided, of course, by authorities. I will never speculate."Rutte also struck a defiant tone during a press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, during which he said that “for every incident in Europe, more support for Ukraine, not less support” will be provided.E.U. unveils new sanctions proposal targeting Russian banks and energyThe European Union on Monday presented a sweeping new sanctions package in a bid to increase economic pressure on Moscow to end the war. The package is set to expand restrictions to a further 60 Russian banks, alongside cryptocurrency and payment platforms. It will also target Russia's energy sector by prohibiting European companies from helping build, operate, or repair Russian energy infrastructure, while restricting Europeans from serving on the governing bodies of companies in Russia.“The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine. And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine,” said European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.The proposed measures also seek to further isolate Moscow by restricting visas for former Russian combatants and banning Russian teams and athletes from competing under the country's flag for any sporting events in the E.U. The European Commission added that it was seeking tighter restrictions on tourist visas, alongside additional measures affecting individual artists.Kaja Kallas, the E.U.’s foreign policy chief, hailed the package and said any such “diplomacy to end Russia’s war needs to be backed up by pressure on the aggressor.”The new set of sanctions will need to be agreed and approved by the 27-member states unanimously before they can come into force.
